final_proof:
Let \(dm\) denote the mass measure of the body, so that \(M=\int_B dm\). Choose the centre of mass as the origin, and let \(\mathbf r\) be the position vector of a mass element. By the defining property of the centre of mass,
\[
\int_B \mathbf r\,dm=\mathbf 0.
\]

Let \(\mathbf u\) be a unit vector parallel to the two axes. Define the orthogonal projection onto the plane perpendicular to the axes by
\[
P\mathbf x=\mathbf x-(\mathbf x\mathbin{\cdot}\mathbf u)\mathbf u.
\]
Since \(A\) passes through the origin, it is the line \(\{t\mathbf u:t\in\mathbb R\}\), and the squared distance of the point \(\mathbf r\) from \(A\) is \(\lVert P\mathbf r\rVert^2\). Hence
\[
I_0=\int_B \lVert P\mathbf r\rVert^2\,dm.
\]

There is a unique shortest displacement vector \(\mathbf a\) from \(A\) to \(A'\). It is perpendicular to \(\mathbf u\), satisfies \(\lVert\mathbf a\rVert=l\), and permits the representation
\[
A'=\{\mathbf a+t\mathbf u:t\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
The squared distance of \(\mathbf r\) from \(A'\) is therefore \(\lVert P(\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\rVert^2\). Since \(P\mathbf a=\mathbf a\), this is \(\lVert P\mathbf r-\mathbf a\rVert^2\). Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
I
&=\int_B \lVert P\mathbf r-\mathbf a\rVert^2\,dm\\
&=\int_B\left(\lVert P\mathbf r\rVert^2-2\mathbf a\mathbin{\cdot}P\mathbf r+\lVert\mathbf a\rVert^2\right)dm\\
&=I_0-2\mathbf a\mathbin{\cdot}\int_B P\mathbf r\,dm+\lVert\mathbf a\rVert^2\int_Bdm.
\end{aligned}
\]
Linearity of \(P\), together with the centre-of-mass identity, gives
\[
\int_B P\mathbf r\,dm=P\left(\int_B\mathbf r\,dm\right)=\mathbf0.
\]
Using also \(\int_Bdm=M\) and \(\lVert\mathbf a\rVert=l\), the preceding formula reduces to
\[
\boxed{I=I_0+Ml^2}.
\]
